summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina lets citizens of the EU, the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and many other countries, including Russia, Turkey, China, Kuwait, Qatar and the UAE, visit visa-free for up to 90 days (30 days for Ukrainians; for Russians, 30 days with a tourist voucher or 90 days with an invitation letter verified by the Service for Foreigners' Affairs), while other travelers need a short-stay visa from a Bosnian embassy or can enter for up to 30 days with a valid multiple-entry Schengen, EU or US visa or residence permit.

conditionalWaivers.text: Holders of a valid multiple-entry visa or a residence permit issued by a Schengen state, an EU member state or the United States can enter Bosnia and Herzegovina visa-free, whatever their nationality. A single uninterrupted stay may last up to 30 days, with up to 90 days in total in any 180-day period, and never beyond the validity of the visa or permit.

passportValidity.text: The UK Foreign Office says your passport must have an expiry date at least 90 days after the date you plan to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a date of issue less than 10 years before the date you arrive. The Government of Canada says it must be valid for at least 3 months beyond the date you expect to leave.

travelInsurance.text: Visa applicants must hold travel insurance covering at least EUR 30,000 (or USD 50,000): the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Qatar lists it among the documents for a visa. No official source we could read states an insurance requirement for visa-free visitors.

The UK Foreign Office says all foreign nationals must register with the police within 72 hours of arrival.

tips.text: The UK FCDO says landmines and other unexploded weapons remain from the 1992–1995 war, mainly in less populated and rural areas, and advises not to step off roads and paved areas without an experienced guide.

Foreign visitors must register with the police soon after arrival — within 72 hours according to the UK FCDO, or within 48 hours for stays of 3 days or more according to the Government of Canada. The FCDO says hotels and some hostels usually register their guests; otherwise contact the nearest field centre of the Service for Foreigners' Affairs.
The Government of Canada says the economy is primarily cash-based and ATMs are limited in rural areas.

If you hold a valid multiple-entry visa or a residence permit from a Schengen state, an EU member state or the United States, you can enter Bosnia and Herzegovina without a Bosnian visa for up to 30 days at a time.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Bosnia and Herzegovina?
faq.answer: Citizens of the EU, the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and many other countries can stay visa-free for up to 90 days, and citizens of EU and Schengen states, Andorra, Montenegro, Liechtenstein, Monaco, San Marino, Serbia, the Holy See, Switzerland, North Macedonia and Albania can enter with a valid identity card. Ukrainian citizens get 30 days within two months of first entry, and Russian citizens 30 days with a tourist voucher or 90 days with an invitation letter verified by the Service for Foreigners' Affairs; Turkey, China, Kuwait, Qatar and the UAE get 90 days. Everyone else needs a short-stay visa from a Bosnian mission, unless they hold a valid multiple-entry visa or residence permit from a Schengen state, an EU member state or the US.

faq.question: Can I enter Bosnia and Herzegovina with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Yes — holders of a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa (or an EU or US one, or a residence permit from any of those) can enter visa-free for up to 30 days at a time, and 90 days in any 180, within the visa's validity, without applying for a Bosnian visa.

faq.question: What currency is used in Bosnia and Herzegovina?
faq.answer: The convertible mark (BAM, written KM). The Government of Canada says the economy is primarily cash-based and ATMs are limited in rural areas.

faq.question: Is Bosnia and Herzegovina safe to visit?
faq.answer: The UK FCDO warns of pickpockets and bag-snatchers in the tourist areas of Sarajevo and other cities, and says landmines and other unexploded weapons remain from the 1992–1995 war in less populated and rural areas. It advises not to step off roads and paved areas without an experienced guide.
